newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ICO sees world 1996/97 coffee output up 18 percent.
newsitem.headline: ICO sees world 1996/97 coffee output up 18 percent.

text.p: World coffee production is expected to rise by about 18 percent to 101 million 60-kg bags in 1996/97 (October/September) from the previous year, the International Coffee Organisation (ICO) said in a report on Tuesday.
The 61-member ICO, which groups leading coffee producing and consuming countries, is holding a three-day meeting on the Indonesian resort island of Bali. The meeting ends on Wednesday.

"Brazilian output of 25.5 million bags in 1996/97 will add about 6.3 percent to world production...if output remains the same in other exporting countries," said the report, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.
It said preliminary data provided by exporting countries showed their output would increase by some 5.8 million bags, about 11 percent more than in 1995/96.
"Thus world production in coffee year 1996/97 can be estimated at around 101 million bags, some 18 percent more than in the previous year," the report said.

It said data from member countries indicated their total production in 1995/96 was 92.7 million bags. This was some 3.2 percent more than the 1994/95 crop which was cut by damage to the Brazilian crop from frost and drought.
The report said although 1996/97 output estimates by some leading producing countries showed an increase, the prospects for world supply would depend largely on Brazil's crop.
Brazil is the world's largest coffee producer, followed by Colombia and Indonesia.
"Nevertheless, looking at the supply fundamentals in detail, it seems likely that availability will continue to be very tight for certain types of coffee," the report said.
It said the world coffee market would continue to experience volatility in a narrow range.

"It should be noted that the differentials between arabica and robusta have considerably increased. This widening of arbitrage reflects a certain perception by the market of the supply for different types of coffee," it said.
"As a result, one needs to look at fundamentals separately and carefully before drawing any broad conclusion," it said.
The report said the gross opening stocks of exporting countries in 1996/97 fell to 36.3 million bags from 39.9 million in 1995/96, due mainly to higher exports.
It said domestic consumption in exporting countries was estimated to grow to 23.5 million bags in 1996/97 from 22.9 million bags in 1995/96.
The report said stocks in importing countries were estimated to be between eight million and nine million bags currently, compared with about 20 million bags in September 1990.
The rate of the decline of stocks showed signs of slowing or even stabilising, it said.

It said the current market backwardation, when the price for spot or near-term delivery of coffee was higher than distant months, reflected the market view that supply would increase in the longer term, which would pressure prices.
